blocks.text: A pituitary gland the size of a pea sits in a bony hollow beneath the brain, and it controls the thyroid, adrenals, gonads, breast, kidney water handling and growth. Yet the pituitary is not the boss: a thin stalk connects it to the hypothalamus, which decides what it releases. Cut that stalk and some hormones fail while one rises, which tells you how the connection works.

blocks.markdown:
**Two glands, two connections.** The pituitary (hypophysis) has two lobes with different origins and different links to the **hypothalamus**.

- **Posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis)** is neural tissue. It is connected to the hypothalamus by **axons**: large (magnocellular) neurons in the **supraoptic** and **paraventricular** nuclei make **antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin)** and **oxytocin**, which travel down the axons of the **hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract** and are stored in nerve terminals. They are released into blood by action potentials, exactly like neurotransmitters.
- **Anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis)** is glandular tissue. It is connected by **blood vessels**. Small (parvocellular) hypothalamic neurons release **releasing and inhibiting hormones** into a capillary plexus at the **median eminence**; these drain through the **hypophyseal portal veins** into a second capillary bed in the anterior pituitary, where they act on endocrine cells. The portal system delivers tiny amounts directly, without dilution in the systemic circulation.

blocks.title: Hypophyseal portal system
blocks.text: A portal system is a vein that links two capillary beds. The hypophyseal portal veins carry hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones from the primary capillary plexus in the median eminence to the secondary plexus in the anterior pituitary. This is the vascular link; the neural link to the posterior pituitary is the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract.

blocks.markdown: **Hypothalamic control of the anterior pituitary.** Five of the six anterior pituitary hormones are mostly stimulated by hypothalamic releasing hormones: **TRH** (thyrotropin-releasing hormone) for TSH (and prolactin), **CRH** for ACTH, **GnRH** for LH and FSH, and **GHRH** for growth hormone. **Somatostatin** inhibits GH release. **Prolactin** is unusual: it is under predominantly **inhibitory** control by **dopamine** from the hypothalamus. Each anterior pituitary hormone also exerts negative feedback, either directly or through its target gland's hormones, on both pituitary and hypothalamus.

blocks.caption: Anterior pituitary hormones and their targets.

blocks.markdown:
**Antidiuretic hormone.** ADH is a nonapeptide released when **plasma osmolality** rises (osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect small rises of 1-2%, and release begins above a threshold of about 280-285 mOsm/kg) or when **blood volume or pressure falls** (baroreceptor input; a larger change is needed). In the kidney, ADH binds **V2 receptors** on collecting duct principal cells, raising cAMP and driving insertion of **aquaporin-2** water channels into the apical membrane. Water is then reabsorbed down the osmotic gradient and urine becomes concentrated. At high concentrations, ADH acts on **V1 receptors** to cause vasoconstriction. Lack of ADH causes **central diabetes insipidus** (large volumes of dilute urine); failure of the kidney to respond causes **nephrogenic diabetes insipidus**.

**Oxytocin** is released in response to nipple stimulation (causing **milk ejection** by contracting myoepithelial cells) and to cervical stretch in labour (causing **uterine contraction**); both are positive feedback reflexes.

blocks.caption: Estimated osmolality with all concentrations in mmol/L; reference range about 275-295 mOsm/kg (laboratories vary).

blocks.title: Estimating plasma osmolality
blocks.prompt: A patient has plasma sodium 142 mmol/L, glucose 5.0 mmol/L and urea 5.5 mmol/L. Estimate the osmolality and say whether ADH secretion would be expected to rise.

steps.text: Double the sodium to account for its accompanying anions.

Compare with the osmotic threshold for ADH release (about 280-285) and the upper reference limit (about 295): the value is at the upper end, so ADH release is strongly stimulated and urine would be concentrated.

blocks.answer: About 294.5 mOsm/kg, at the upper end of normal, so ADH secretion would be expected to be high.

blocks.title: How ADH sets urine volume
blocks.prompt: An adult must excrete a solute load of 800 mOsm per day. Calculate the daily urine volume if urine osmolality is 400 mOsm/kg (taking 1 kg as 1 L), and if it is limited to 100 mOsm/kg in ADH deficiency.

steps.text: Volume equals solute load divided by urine osmolality.
With ADH absent, urine osmolality is only 100 mOsm/kg.
The fourfold difference illustrates why ADH deficiency causes polyuria, thirst and polydipsia.

blocks.answer: 2.0 L/day with urine at 400 mOsm/kg, but 8.0 L/day when urine cannot be concentrated beyond 100 mOsm/kg.

items: Posterior pituitary: neural link; ADH and oxytocin made in supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei and released from nerve terminals.
Anterior pituitary: vascular link through hypophyseal portal veins carrying releasing and inhibiting hormones.
Anterior hormones: GH, prolactin, ACTH, TSH, LH, FSH; prolactin is tonically inhibited by dopamine.
ADH: V2 receptors, aquaporin-2 in collecting duct; stimulated by raised osmolality or low volume.
Oxytocin: milk ejection and uterine contraction.

blocks.title: What stalk damage teaches
blocks.text: If the pituitary stalk is cut (by trauma or tumour), the anterior pituitary loses its releasing hormones, so GH, ACTH, TSH and gonadotrophins fall, but prolactin rises because it loses its inhibitory dopamine. ADH secretion may also fall, causing diabetes insipidus, because ADH-producing axons are damaged.

blocks.title: Posterior pituitary hormones are not made there
blocks.text: ADH and oxytocin are synthesised in the hypothalamus; the posterior pituitary only stores and releases them. Damage to the posterior pituitary alone can therefore cause only a temporary deficiency if the hypothalamic cell bodies survive.

points: The posterior pituitary is linked to the hypothalamus by axons carrying ADH and oxytocin; the anterior pituitary is linked by portal blood carrying releasing and inhibiting hormones.
The anterior pituitary secretes GH, prolactin, ACTH, TSH, LH and FSH, each with a defined target; prolactin is controlled mainly by inhibitory dopamine.
ADH acts on V2 receptors in the collecting duct to insert aquaporin-2 and conserve water when plasma osmolality rises or volume falls.
Oxytocin causes uterine contraction and milk ejection, both through positive feedback reflexes.

questions.stem: Where are antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin synthesised?

options.text: In neurons of the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus
In the cells of the posterior pituitary itself
In the cells of the anterior pituitary

questions.correctOptionText: In neurons of the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the hormones travel down axons to be stored in the posterior pituitary.
distractorRationale.b: The posterior pituitary stores and releases them but does not synthesise them.
distractorRationale.c: The anterior pituitary makes GH, PRL, ACTH, TSH, LH and FSH.

questions.explanation: ADH and oxytocin are made in hypothalamic magnocellular neurons and travel along the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract to nerve terminals in the posterior pituitary. This neural link contrasts with the vascular portal link to the anterior pituitary.

questions.stem: How do hypothalamic releasing hormones reach the cells of the anterior pituitary?

options.text: Through the hypophyseal portal veins from the median eminence
By axonal transport down the pituitary stalk
Through the systemic circulation from the heart

questions.correctOptionText: Through the hypophyseal portal veins from the median eminence

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the portal system is the vascular link.
distractorRationale.b: Axonal transport is the route for the posterior pituitary hormones.
distractorRationale.c: Cerebrospinal fluid is not the route of delivery.
distractorRationale.d: The portal system delivers hormones directly without systemic dilution.

questions.explanation: Releasing and inhibiting hormones are secreted into a capillary plexus at the median eminence and flow through portal veins to a second capillary bed in the anterior pituitary. This arrangement delivers small amounts directly to target cells.

questions.stem: What is the principal cellular action of ADH on the collecting duct principal cell?

options.text: V2 receptor activation raising cAMP and inserting aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane
V1 receptor activation causing vasodilation of the afferent arteriole
Inhibition of the Na+/K+ ATPase in the loop of Henle
Stimulation of aldosterone release from the adrenal cortex

questions.correctOptionText: V2 receptor activation raising cAMP and inserting aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane

distractorRationale.a: Correct: more aquaporin-2 means more water reabsorption and concentrated urine.
distractorRationale.b: V1 activation causes vasoconstriction, not vasodilation.
distractorRationale.c: ADH does not act by inhibiting this pump.
distractorRationale.d: ADH does not stimulate aldosterone release.

questions.explanation: ADH binds V2 receptors, which raises cAMP and drives insertion of aquaporin-2 channels into the apical membrane. Water then leaves the tubule down the osmotic gradient, concentrating the urine.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man develops severe thirst and passes 9 L of dilute urine daily after a head injury. Plasma osmolality is high and urine osmolality is low, rising markedly after a dose of desmopressin (an ADH analogue; pharmacology teaching example). What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Central diabetes insipidus from deficient ADH release
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus from renal unresponsiveness to ADH

questions.correctOptionText: Central diabetes insipidus from deficient ADH release

distractorRationale.a: Correct: urine concentrates in response to exogenous ADH, so the kidney is responsive but ADH is lacking.
distractorRationale.b: In nephrogenic disease urine would not concentrate after desmopressin.
distractorRationale.c: Primary polydipsia gives low plasma osmolality, not high.
distractorRationale.d: Excess ADH gives concentrated urine and low plasma osmolality.

questions.explanation: Head injury can damage the hypothalamus or stalk and reduce ADH release, producing large volumes of dilute urine and a high plasma osmolality. Urine concentrating in response to desmopressin shows the collecting duct is responsive, so the defect is central.

questions.stem: After section of the pituitary stalk, plasma prolactin falls because the anterior pituitary loses its releasing hormones.
questions.explanation: Prolactin is under predominantly inhibitory control by hypothalamic dopamine delivered by the portal vessels. When the stalk is cut, this inhibition is lost and prolactin rises, whereas GH, ACTH, TSH and the gonadotrophins fall.

questions.stem: A patient has plasma sodium 150 mmol/L, glucose 5.5 mmol/L and urea 8.5 mmol/L. Using osmolality = 2 x [Na+] + [glucose] + [urea], calculate the estimated plasma osmolality in mOsm/kg.
questions.explanation: Osmolality is 2 x 150 + 5.5 + 8.5 = 300 + 14 = 314 mOsm/kg. This is well above the usual upper reference limit of about 295, a strong stimulus for ADH release; if urine is also dilute, ADH deficiency or resistance is suspected.

questions.stem: A patient must excrete a solute load of 600 mOsm per day. Because of ADH deficiency, urine osmolality cannot exceed 80 mOsm/kg. Taking 1 kg of urine as 1 L, what is the minimum daily urine volume in litres?
questions.explanation: Volume equals solute load divided by urine osmolality: 600 / 80 = 7.5 L/day. With intact ADH a urine osmolality of 600 mOsm/kg or more would reduce the volume to about 1 L/day.

questions.stem: Contrast the neural link between the hypothalamus and posterior pituitary with the vascular link to the anterior pituitary, naming the hormones and the structures involved in each.
markingGuide: Posterior pituitary: neural link by axons of magnocellular neurons of the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei in the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract
ADH and oxytocin are made in the hypothalamus, stored in posterior pituitary terminals and released by action potentials
Anterior pituitary: vascular link by the hypophyseal portal system
Parvocellular neurons release releasing/inhibiting hormones (TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH, somatostatin, dopamine) into the median eminence capillary plexus
Portal veins carry them to the secondary plexus in the anterior pituitary, acting on endocrine cells
questions.explanation: The two lobes differ in embryology and in how they are controlled. A neural connection suits hormones released on demand from nerve terminals, whereas a portal connection delivers tiny quantities of regulators directly to gland cells.

questions.stem: List the six anterior pituitary hormones, give the main target of each, and state which hypothalamic hormone predominantly inhibits one of them.
markingGuide: GH: liver (IGF-1) and tissues, growth and metabolism
TSH: thyroid gland, thyroid hormone synthesis and release
LH and FSH: gonads (sex steroids, ovulation, spermatogenesis, follicle development)
Prolactin is tonically inhibited by hypothalamic dopamine (somatostatin also inhibits GH)
questions.explanation: Each anterior hormone acts on a specific target and is controlled by hypothalamic releasing or inhibiting hormones plus negative feedback. Prolactin is the exception that is under predominantly inhibitory control.

questions.stem: Explain what stimulates ADH secretion, how ADH acts on the kidney, and what distinguishes central from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. State the actions of oxytocin.
markingGuide: ADH release is stimulated by raised plasma osmolality (hypothalamic osmoreceptors) and by reduced blood volume or pressure (baroreceptors)
ADH binds V2 receptors on collecting duct principal cells, raising cAMP and inserting aquaporin-2 so water is reabsorbed and urine concentrated
At high concentrations V1 receptors cause vasoconstriction
Central diabetes insipidus: deficient ADH production or release; urine concentrates after desmopressin
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus: kidney is unresponsive to ADH; urine does not concentrate after desmopressin
Oxytocin causes uterine contraction and milk ejection by myoepithelial cell contraction (positive feedback reflexes)
questions.explanation: ADH regulates water balance by controlling aquaporin-2 insertion, so lack of the hormone or its receptor response leads to polyuria. A desmopressin test separates deficiency from resistance.
